focus.text: Good writing keeps the reader inside one time frame and only moves when it says so. Pick the frame your paragraph lives in, past for a story, present for an argument, future for a plan, and keep the verbs there. Then, when you really do need to move, put a time word at the front of the sentence and change the verb form with it. Readers forgive a shift they can see coming; they get lost when the verbs move on their own.

summaryTable.caption: The frame each kind of writing usually lives in
rows: back to the past perfect for earlier background
present perfect or simple past for evidence
present forms in time clauses and arrangements
simple past for the period covered
simple present for what the chart itself shows

pretest.sentence: Last Sunday we cleaned the beach at Mỹ Khê, and we collected forty bags of plastic.
pretest.reason: Both events sit in the same finished past frame.

pretest.sentence: Yesterday I met my old teacher at the market, and she asks me about my exams.
pretest.reason: The sentence is in the past frame (*yesterday*, *met*), so write *she asked*.

pretest.sentence: The chart shows the number of visitors, which rose sharply after 2015.
pretest.reason: The chart *shows* now, while the data belongs to a finished period.

pretest.sentence: In my opinion, schools should teach cooking. It was a skill that everybody needed.
pretest.reason: The argument is about now, so keep the present: *It is a skill that everybody needs*.

pretest.sentence: When I was younger, I hated writing essays, but now I enjoy them.
pretest.reason: *When I was younger* and *now* signal the shift, so the change of form is clear.

pretest.sentence: Since 2019 the school opened three new clubs.
pretest.reason: *Since 2019* reaches up to now, so use the present perfect: *has opened*.

pretest.sentence: Last year I have visited my grandparents in Nam Định twice.
pretest.reason: *Last year* is a finished time, so use the simple past: *visited*.

pretest.sentence: The lights went out at nine. We had already finished dinner, so we lit a candle.
pretest.reason: The past perfect marks the background that happened before the main event.

pretest.sentence: Tomorrow the volunteers meet at seven, and by noon they will have painted the whole wall.
pretest.reason: A fixed schedule stays in the simple present, while the deadline takes the future perfect.

pretest.sentence: While the guide explained the history, a student is taking notes.
pretest.reason: Both actions belong to the same past scene, so write *was taking*.

context.title: From a market stall to an online shop
context.paragraph: My aunt opened a small fabric shop in Huế in 2010. For the first few years she sold only to neighbours, and she had never used a computer for work. Then the pandemic closed the market for several months. While the shop was shut, my cousin taught her how to photograph the fabric and post it online. Today my aunt runs the shop and an online page, and she sends parcels all over the country. She has trained two young assistants since last summer, and next year she is going to open a second page in English. She still says the old market taught her more than any course.

sections.title: Forming a time frame

table.caption: The forms that belong to each time frame
rows: *we will open* / *we are going to open*

notes: Each row is one frame. Inside a frame you can move between the columns freely; jumping to another row needs a time word that tells the reader why.

items.stem: Our school opened in 1998. At that time it ___ only four classrooms.
items.reason: The sentence stays in the past frame set by *in 1998*.

items.stem: Air pollution is a serious problem in big cities. Every year the number of vehicles ___.
items.reason: A general argument about now stays in the present frame.

items.stem: By the time the teacher came in, the class ___ the whiteboard.
items.reason: The cleaning happened before she came in, so it takes the past perfect.

items.stem: The festival starts on Friday. By Sunday evening the organisers ___ ten thousand tickets.
items.reason: The frame is future, so an action finished before Sunday takes the future perfect.

items.stem: I have lived in Cần Thơ for six years. I ___ here in 2020 with my parents.
items.reason: *In 2020* is a finished time, so the sentence shifts to the simple past.

sections.title: Forming a shift: time words and the form they bring

table.caption: Time words and the verb form that usually follows them
rows: *since, so far, already, up to now*
Prices **had fallen** before the new rule arrived.

notes: Put the time word first when you change frame: *In 2019 the club had twelve members. Today it has more than a hundred.*

items.sentence: Last winter the lake freezes for three days, and children skated on it.
items.reason: *Last winter* sets a past frame, so the verb stays past.

items.sentence: So far this term our class collected more than sixty kilograms of paper.
items.reason: *So far this term* is an unfinished period, so it takes the present perfect.

items.sentence: The report explains the survey and showed that most students walk to school.
items.reason: The report *explains* and *shows* now, so keep one present frame.

items.sentence: When the bell rang, we already packed our bags.
items.reason: The packing happened before the bell, so it needs the past perfect.

items.sentence: Two years ago the village has installed solar panels on the school roof.
items.reason: *Two years ago* is a finished time, so use the simple past.

sections.title: Using one frame at a time

rules.text: Decide the frame before you start. A story or a report of events lives in the past; an opinion or a description of how things work lives in the present.

examples.text: We **interviewed** twenty families in April, and most of them **agreed** to help again.
Homework **divides** opinion, and many parents **believe** it teaches discipline.

rules.text: Do not change the verb form only because a new sentence starts. If nothing in the meaning has moved, the form should not move either.

examples.text: Last term we ran a book club. Every Friday we **met** in the library and **swapped** novels.

rules.text: In an essay, use the simple present for your ideas and the simple past for a specific piece of evidence from a finished time.

examples.text: Cycling **reduces** traffic. In 2022 a scheme in Hà Nội **cut** journey times by ten per cent.

tips: Read your draft and underline every verb. If two verbs next to each other sit in different frames, one of them is probably a slip rather than a shift.

sections.title: Using time words to signal a shift

rules.text: Signal a shift with a time expression at the front of the sentence, then change the verb form.

examples.text: **Ten years ago** the beach **was** almost empty. **Today** it **attracts** thousands of visitors.

rules.text: Keep the shift short. Move, say what you need to say, then come back to the main frame.

examples.text: The programme **works** well. It **started** in 2019 with two schools, and it now **covers** the district.

rules.text: *Now*, *these days* and *at present* pull a sentence into the present; *then*, *at that time* and *in those days* push it into the past.

examples.text: **In those days** students **copied** notes by hand; **these days** they **photograph** the board.

notes: A shift needs a reason the reader can see. Without a time word, a new verb form simply looks like a mistake.

sections.title: Using background and main events across a paragraph

timeline.label: The background runs behind the story; the main events are the points that move it forward.

rules.text: In a narrative, put the main events in the simple past and the background in the past progressive.

examples.text: It **was raining** heavily when the coach **arrived** at the station.

rules.text: Use the past perfect only for what happened before your main events, and drop back to the simple past as soon as the story moves forward again.

examples.text: The club **had lost** two players before the season **began**, so the coach changed the plan.

rules.text: In a discussion essay, keep the present for your claims and use the present perfect for change that still matters.

examples.text: Online courses **are** now common. Universities **have opened** hundreds of free programmes since 2015.

rules.text: When you describe past data, keep the past for the period and the present for what the figures themselves show.

examples.text: The graph **shows** that rice exports **fell** between 2018 and 2021.

tips: A paragraph with three frames in five sentences is hard to follow. Two frames, with one clear time word between them, is usually enough.

sentences: The last bus left at six.
We reached the stop at ten past six.
model: By the time we reached the stop, the last bus had left.
The last bus had already left when we reached the stop.
items.focus: past perfect for the earlier event
items.reason: The bus left first, so it takes the past perfect while the later event stays in the simple past.

sentences: The club started with twelve members in 2018.
It has more than a hundred members now.
model: The club started with twelve members in 2018, and today it has more than a hundred.
Since 2018 the club has grown from twelve members to more than a hundred.
items.focus: signalling a shift from past to present
items.reason: A time word (*in 2018*, *today*, *since 2018*) makes the change of frame visible to the reader.

model: While I was cooking dinner, the power went off.
I was cooking dinner when the power went off.
items.focus: background in the past progressive, main event in the simple past
items.reason: The longer action is the background, so it takes the past progressive.

sentences: We finished the survey in March.
We will publish the results next month.
model: We finished the survey in March, and we will publish the results next month.
We finished the survey in March; the results will appear next month.
items.focus: moving from a past frame to a future one
items.reason: Each clause carries its own time word, so the move from past to future is clear.

sentences: Many families used to cook with coal.
Most families use gas or electricity today.
model: Many families used to cook with coal, but most of them use gas or electricity today.
In the past families cooked with coal; today most of them use gas or electricity.
items.focus: *used to* for a past habit that has changed
items.reason: *Used to* marks the old habit, and *today* signals the move into the present frame.

editing.text: Our school started a paper recycling project three years ago, and it has changed the way we think about waste. At the beginning only one class take part, and we collected about ten kilograms a week. In the first year we had one big problem: nobody want to carry the heavy boxes to the store room. Then our teacher builds a small trolley with the technology club, and the job became much easier. Since that day every class joined the project. Today the school collect almost two hundred kilograms a month, and last term we have sold the paper to a mill in the next district. Next year we are going to buy a second trolley when we will have enough money, and we will invite the primary school next door to join us.

errors.reason: *At the beginning* of a past story needs the simple past *took*.
The paragraph is in the past frame (*In the first year*), so the verb stays past.
*Then* continues the past narrative, so use the simple past.

errors.span: Since that day every class joined
errors.fix: Since that day every class has joined
errors.reason: *Since that day* runs up to now, so the present perfect keeps the period open.
*The school* is it, so the present verb takes -s.
*Last term* is a finished time, so use the simple past.

errors.span: when we will have enough money
errors.reason: A *when* clause about the future takes the present.

topics.prompt: Write to a friend about a journey that went wrong. Say what you had planned before you left, what happened on the day, and what you do differently now.
checklist: The story keeps one past frame from beginning to end.
The background before the journey uses the past perfect.
Any move into the present is introduced by a time word such as *now* or *these days*.

topics.prompt: "Schools should teach students how to manage money." Give your view, and support it with one example from your own experience.
checklist: Your claims stay in the simple present.
The example from your own life shifts into the past with a time word in front of it.
No verb changes frame without a reason the reader can see.

topics.prompt: Describe how a street, market or neighbourhood you know has changed. Cover what it was like before, what it is like now, and what will happen to it next.
checklist: Each part of the description names its time frame before the verbs change.
The present perfect is used for changes that still matter today.
Future plans use *will* or *be going to*, and time clauses keep a present form.
